case_study_insert.main_stem: Fairway Road Freight (FRG) is a partnership in the road haulage and freight transport sector, employing a workforce of 40. Founded in 2008 by Callum Reid, it operates a flat structure with democratic leadership. FRG plans to invest $500,000 in a fleet of low-emission articulated lorries with telematics, financed by a $300,000 five-year bank loan and $200,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $180,000 a year, a variable cost of $6 a unit and a selling price of $16, and currently produces 45,000 units a year. FRG also faces driver absenteeism of 7% and rising vehicle downtime from breakdowns, and the partners aim to cut breakdowns and retain their regional haulage contracts.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Operations Report — Q3 2025: FRG completed 11,000 deliveries last quarter with an on-time rate of 91.5%, down from 95.2% a year ago. Damage claims rose from 19 to 31 per month, and average delivery time is 2.8 days. A survey of 300 haulage customers found that 64% value a low-emission fleet and 58% would pay $0.80 more for greener freight. A fleet audit shows 14 of 40 drivers need telematics training; an external course costs $600 per driver.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Fairway Road Freight for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 3.8% to 4.6%, raising borrowing costs for firms with variable-rate loans. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 5.4% from $13.20 to $13.91 per hour from April 2027. (3) Diesel and tyre input costs have risen 10.2% year-on-year, while road-freight volumes grew 3.3% over the same period.

questions.question_text: FRG is funding part of its lorry-fleet expansion with a five-year bank loan. Explain two advantages for FRG of using retained profit instead of the bank loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Retained profit needs no interest charges or fixed repayments, so FRG keeps the cash that would otherwise service the $300,000 five-year bank loan. That cash can cover fixed costs of $180,000 a year and the running of the new $500,000 low-emission fleet while driver absenteeism of 7% and rising breakdowns are adding cost. Every dollar saved in interest can be spent on telematics or on reducing the 31 monthly damage claims, helping FRG retain its regional haulage contracts without raising the $16 selling price.

Point 2: Using $200,000 retained profit keeps control with Callum Reid and the other partners rather than a lender, so no bank can dictate how the lorries or the telematics system are run. It also avoids pledging partnership assets while vehicle downtime is high and the 14 drivers still need $600 training. The survey evidence that 64% of customers value a low-emission fleet and 58% would pay $0.80 more shows where internally saved cash can be reinvested, rather than paid as interest that competes with the $180,000 fixed costs and the cost of the fleet expansion.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual explanation and analysis applied to FRG and its financing decision.

questions.question_text: FRG is promoting its low-emission lorry fleet. Consider a national trade-press campaign, local radio sponsorship, or targeted social media and livery branding. Which should FRG choose? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
National trade-press campaign: Advertisements in haulage magazines and online trade titles could reach freight managers across the country and build credibility for FRG's low-emission fleet. However, design and media costs are high for a 40-employee partnership already servicing a $300,000 loan and investing $500,000, and print ads cannot demonstrate the telematics that 64% of surveyed customers value. Much of the readership will not be in FRG's regional catchment.

Local radio sponsorship: Sponsorship of regional radio is cheaper and reaches the local catchment where FRG's 11,000 quarterly deliveries are made, so it suits a quick message about greener freight. Its weakness is narrow reach and short-lived impact: listeners are not necessarily the 300 haulage customers in the survey, and with a 91.5% on-time rate the message should demonstrate reliability rather than simply announce it.

Targeted social media and livery branding: Posts aimed at freight managers, plus clear branding on the articulated lorries themselves, reach the people who award haulage contracts and visibly demonstrate the low-emission fleet on the road. This is low cost per contact and measurable, and it reinforces the 58% who would pay $0.80 more for greener freight; sharing live telematics data can also answer concerns about the 31 monthly damage claims and 2.8-day delivery time.

Recommendation: FRG should choose targeted social media and livery branding. It reaches the exact decision-makers, costs far less than trade press and works beyond a single local radio area. Trade press is rejected as costly and untargeted for a 40-person partnership funding a $300,000 loan; radio is rejected as too narrow and fleeting for customers spread across regional supply chains. Social media lacks the authority of trade press, so FRG should add a small trade-press listing once the 7% absenteeism and breakdown rate are under control.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited outline of the promotional options with minimal application to FRG.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of at least two options in the context of FRG with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options with a well-justified recommendation explaining why trade press and radio are rejected.

questions.question_text: FRG has driver absenteeism of 7% and rising vehicle downtime. Explain two benefits for FRG of using democratic leadership within its flat structure to motivate its drivers.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Democratic leadership lets the 40 employees help decide route schedules and vehicle-check routines, so their practical knowledge can reduce the breakdowns behind FRG's falling 91.5% on-time rate. In a flat structure, suggestions reach Callum Reid and the other partners directly, raising commitment and helping to lower the 7% absenteeism rate that leaves lorries without drivers.

Point 2: Involving drivers in decisions about the new $500,000 telematics lorries makes the 14 needing training more willing to learn the $600 course, because they understand why the data matters. Shared ideas on loading can also reduce the 31 monthly damage claims and protect the 2.8-day delivery target. With a $300,000 loan to service, motivation that cuts absenteeism protects the 45,000-unit output and keeps the 64% of customers who value a low-emission fleet satisfied. Democratic leadership suits an experienced driver group whose local knowledge improves reliability, though the partners must still set firm safety and maintenance standards to bring downtime down.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to FRG's absenteeism, downtime and fleet investment.

questions.question_text: FRG wants to cut its 7% absenteeism and falling 91.5% on-time rate. Consider a performance-related bonus or job enrichment through team working. Which should FRG choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
Performance-related bonus: Paying drivers for attendance and on-time deliveries could motivate the 40 staff to lift the 91.5% on-time rate back toward 95.2% and reduce the 7% absenteeism, and it is easy to measure against the 11,000 quarterly deliveries. However, the insert gives no bonus cost, so its expense cannot be calculated; it would add to fixed costs of $180,000 a year while FRG services a $300,000 loan and funds a $500,000 fleet. A bonus pays after the event and does not fix the vehicle breakdowns causing downtime.

Job enrichment through team working: Giving drivers varied routes, shared responsibility for vehicle checks and a say in loading routines makes the work less repetitive and uses their local knowledge, which can reduce the 31 monthly damage claims and improve the 2.8-day delivery target. Teams can share the $600 telematics training, with the 14 trained drivers coaching others, and shared ownership can reduce the 7% absenteeism by tackling its cause. The drawback is the time needed to organise teams and agree standards in a flat structure.

Decision: FRG should choose job enrichment through team working. It addresses the causes of absenteeism and poor punctuality rather than paying around them, costs little compared with a bonus whose size is unstated, and helps the 14 drivers learn telematics through their colleagues. The bonus is rejected as an expensive short-term payment that does not change working methods or fix breakdowns, though a small bonus could be added later once reliability improves. With no stated bonus rate the comparison is qualitative: team working changes how the 40 drivers work, while a bonus only rewards results after they occur and competes with $180,000 of fixed costs and the $300,000 loan.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of a bonus and job enrichment with limited application to FRG.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of both options in the context of FRG.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both options with a well-justified decision covering absenteeism, reliability, cost and motivation.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how FRG's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $180,000 ÷ ($16 − $6) = $180,000 ÷ $10 = 18,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 18,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $16 − $6 = $10. Answer: contribution per unit is $10.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways FRG's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Compare the 18,000-unit break-even output with 45,000 units delivered, giving a margin of safety of 27,000 units, so the partners can see how far volumes could fall before the $500,000 fleet stops covering costs.
2. Use the $10 contribution per unit to test the $0.80 premium that 58% of customers would pay: raising price to $16.80 gives $10.80 contribution and lowers break-even to about 16,667 units (180,000 ÷ 10.80).
3. Average total cost is $10.00 a unit ($180,000 ÷ 45,000 = $4.00 plus $6), below the $16 price, leaving room to absorb the 10.2% rise in diesel and tyre costs without an immediate price rise.
4. Labour productivity is 1,125 units per worker (45,000 ÷ 40), a benchmark for checking whether telematics training and team working lift deliveries despite 7% absenteeism.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 18,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $10 | (iii) Four contextual uses: margin of safety of 27,000 units; a $0.80 premium lifting contribution to $10.80 and lowering break-even to about 16,667 units; average total cost of $10.00 against the $16 price; labour productivity of 1,125 units per worker.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method and 1 mark for the accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii); 1 mark for each valid applied use in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate FRG's financial position by calculating the gross profit margin and the profit margin for 2024 and 2025. Has FRG's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Gross Profit Margin 2024 = 37.5%
Gross Profit Margin 2025 = 40.0%
Profit Margin 2024 = 15.0%
Profit Margin 2025 = 17.0%
ROCE 2024 = 15.0%
ROCE 2025 = 18.0%

Detailed workings: 2024 revenue 720, cost of sales 450, gross profit 270; operating profit 108; capital employed 720. 2025 revenue 900, cost of sales 540, gross profit 360; operating profit 153; capital employed 850. Gross profit ÷ revenue: 270 ÷ 720 and 360 ÷ 900. Operating profit ÷ revenue: 108 ÷ 720 and 153 ÷ 900. Operating profit ÷ capital employed: 108 ÷ 720 and 153 ÷ 850.

Evaluation: Every measure is higher in 2025. The share of revenue left after direct costs rose from 37.5% to 40.0% because revenue grew by 180 while cost of sales rose by only 90, so the haulage operation is becoming more efficient even with the 91.5% on-time rate and downtime problems. The share retained as operating profit also rose, and the return on the 850 of capital employed improved, which matters because FRG must service a $300,000 loan while investing $500,000 in new lorries. Interest payable of 20 in 2025 is modest beside operating profit of 153, so financing costs are not undermining the gain. The 7% absenteeism and 31 monthly damage claims remain risks that could reverse the trend if service quality slips.

Conclusion: FRG's financial position has improved. Both margins and the return on capital are higher, with revenue growing faster than cost of sales. The partners should use the stronger margins to fund telematics training and vehicle maintenance so that absenteeism and breakdowns do not erase the improvement.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the two margins for both years with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate calculations for both years, detailed evaluation of revenue, cost, profit and capital trends, and a justified conclusion on whether FRG improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for FRG of introducing low-emission articulated lorries with telematics.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: The survey of 300 haulage customers found that 64% value a low-emission fleet and 58% would pay $0.80 more for greener freight, so the new lorries can help FRG win contracts and add contribution above the $6 variable cost per unit. Telematics data can also tackle the 31 monthly damage claims and the fall to 91.5% on-time delivery, protecting the $16 selling price and the 45,000-unit output.

Disadvantage: The $500,000 fleet must be financed alongside a $300,000 loan, and the 14 drivers needing $600 telematics training cannot use the system fully until trained, which is difficult with 7% absenteeism. The insert gives no figure for low-emission fuel, maintenance or charging, so the exact running-cost saving cannot be calculated; only a qualitative judgement is possible. If telematics data is not acted on, the 11,000 quarterly deliveries and 2.8-day delivery promise may not improve, so the benefit depends on management using the information and on the 58% premium being accepted across contracts.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to FRG's survey, service quality and costs.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the base interest rate rise to 4.6%, the 5.4% minimum wage increase to $13.91 and the 10.2% rise in diesel and tyre costs will affect FRG. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (3.8% to 4.6%): If FRG's $300,000 five-year bank loan is variable-rate, the extra annual interest is 0.8% × $300,000 = $2,400 a year, shown as 0.008 × $300,000. That is small against $180,000 of fixed costs, and if the loan is fixed the direct cost is zero. Higher rates may still slow the 3.3% growth in road-freight volumes.

Minimum wage increase (5.4% to $13.91 an hour): The insert gives no hours worked or current pay, so an annual wage cost cannot be invented. The derived measure is productivity: 45,000 units ÷ 40 workers = 1,125 units per worker. If that holds, the wage rise can be absorbed; if the 7% absenteeism and falling 91.5% on-time rate reduce effective output, unit labour costs rise and the $10 contribution falls. The direction is clear but the size cannot be quantified here.

Input-cost inflation (10.2%): The $6 variable cost is not split into components, so an explicit upper bound is 10.2% × $6 = $0.612, about $0.61 per unit. Across 45,000 units that is 45,000 × $0.61 = $27,450 a year. Even a smaller rise cuts contribution from $10 toward about $9.39 and pushes the break-even output above 18,000 units.

Conclusion: The 10.2% rise in diesel and tyre costs will have the greatest impact. It applies to every one of the 45,000 units and directly erodes the $10 contribution that must cover $180,000 fixed costs and service the $300,000 loan, whereas the interest rise is about $2,400 and the wage effect is unquantifiable and partly offset by productivity. FRG can recover part of it through the $0.80 premium that 58% of customers accept, but breakdowns and downtime already threaten the 91.5% on-time rate.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to FRG.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on FRG's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three changes with shown derivations from insert figures and a well-justified greatest-impact judgement.
